I can't even put into words how awful the local hockey scene has become. When I played in the 90's, it was barren. It is 10 times worse now.

A lot of reasons could go into it; hockey costs increasing faster than inflation, the general decline in youth sports participation, and competition from other rising sports (lacrosse primarily).

However, there are also three other less clear issues; the closure and demolition of the gardens took out two ice sheets. There were plans to replace them...but that obviously never materialized. Second, I'm of the opinion that having two pro hockey teams in this city had a major effect of actually reducing interest in the sport. Both teams had their die-hards, but eventually the casual fan, with too much choice, just stopped caring. Third, and most insidious, was the fact that the youth hockey organization(s) have done a piss poor job of promoting the sport.

CAHA had been around for ages, but eventually, a rival org sprung up. Both sides were more interested in competing to survive, that in my opinion, the entire idea of supporting kids in hockey became secondary. Both orgs eventually merged again, but it's a shell of what even CAHA was. Now, the best hockey orgs in the area are in Oxford and in Northern Kentucky (NKY was a backwater in the 90's).

So, the truth is that the kids don't care about hockey anymore, thus the parents aren't interested. Despite that, the Clones are doing great compared to the rest of the league (their attendance is pretty good).

What I do want to see them do is step back into contributing to youth hockey. That would make them as big as they were in the 90's.

At the very basic; imagine that your enemies can no longer communicate, so the electronic warfare unit that picks you up can't tell the military base to launch interceptors.

Or imagine that missiles using command guidance suddenly can't phone home, and go dumb (the basis for one of our ways of jamming surface-to-air missiles in Vietnam).

Or even imagine that interceptors heading for the strike package you're protecting suddenly see 80 different targets on their scopes, overwhelming their radar systems and situational awareness.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_warfare?scrlybrkr=c1e4c091

I don't have a great grasp of the technical side of things, but on the tactical, a really good electronic warfare environment renders enemy defenses almost moot.

Let's say you're attacking a surface-to-air missile site, with protecting batteries of other surface-to-air missile systems, and under the umbrella of the primary system are mobile surface-to-air missile sites that can pop up.

The package is 4 strike jets, 4 escorts, 2 suppression of enemy air defense jets, and a dedicated electronic warfare jet with a 2 ship escort of its own.

The electronic warfare aircraft is going to focus on the primary surface-to-air missile system, which will be the deadliest and most visible foe. It's probably going to work with the suppression jets to pick up and reflexively jam the pop-up mobile sites as well. When they bring their radars up, the electronic warfare jets jam, the suppression jets do menacing things, and one way or another, the mobile sites go silent. The strike package arrives over the target, the electronic warfare aircraft pounds away at the local defenses by overwhelming, confusing, or harassing any radar-directed systems. Meanwhile, the electronic warfare systems are also jamming away at communications systems, preventing coordination of defenses, including the introduction of fighters into the mix in a timely fashion.

The downside is that, once electronic warfare goes active, the enemy knows something's out there. If all goes well, they don't know any of the Ws (who, what, where, when, why), but they know the general idea that something's going on, and they can always pick up on a couple of the Ws through sheer dumb luck.
